gotcha_text: Landlords use vague relocation language to force dental practices into inferior, non-specialized spaces that lack necessary plumbing or electrical infrastructure. This allows them to reconfigure the building for higher-rent tenants while leaving the dentist with massive, unbudgeted build-out costs.
fix_text: Tenant Pulse identifies ambiguous relocation triggers and flags clauses that lack mandatory landlord-funded build-out provisions. Our tool provides precise language to ensure any move is to a functionally equivalent space at the landlord's sole expense.
deep_dive_html:
The Hidden Cost of Suite Reconfiguration

For dental practitioners, a lease is not merely a right to occupy space; it is a commitment to highly specialized, high-cost infrastructure. Relocation clauses, often buried in the 'Miscellaneous' or 'Expansion' sections, grant landlords the unilateral power to move your practice to a different suite within the center. The danger lies in predatory phrasing—terms like 'at Landlord's sole discretion' or 'to a comparable space' that lack technical, clinical definitions.

In a standard retail lease, 'comparable' might only refer to square footage and storefront visibility. For a dental office, however, a space is only comparable if it maintains the functional integrity of your clinical operations. A landlord can exploit vague language to move you to a space that lacks the necessary utility density, effectively forcing a catastrophic, unbudgeted build-out that can jeopardize your practice's solvency.

To protect your practice, your lease must define 'comparability' through specific, non-negotiable technical benchmarks:

  • Adequate plumbing and specialized drainage for dental chairs, vacuum systems, and sterilization units.
  • Structural capacity for heavy X-ray shielding, lead-lined walls, and specialized imaging equipment.
  • Proximity to specific utility access, including high-voltage electrical requirements and medical-grade air filtration.
  • Visibility, signage prominence, and accessibility consistent with the original suite's foot traffic and parking proximity.

Furthermore, any relocation clause must be paired with a 'Make-Good' provision. This requires the landlord to bear 100% of all construction, permitting, and moving costs, ensuring that the transition does not drain your practice's capital. You must also negotiate for 'Business Interruption' compensation to cover lost revenue during the transition period. Without these protections, a landlord's reconfiguration strategy becomes a direct, unmitigated threat to your practice's operational stability.

title: Predatory Phrasing in Relocation Clauses for Dental Offices
